subtopic_detail: Newly diagnosed ITP with wet purpura
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 4-year-old boy brought by his mother because he woke this morning with numerous small purple spots on his legs and trunk, and this afternoon developed a nosebleed that lasted 20 minutes needing pressure. Two weeks ago he had a viral upper respiratory tract infection which has resolved. He looks systemically well, active, and afebrile.

Examination reveals scattered petechiae over the trunk and limbs, three small ecchymoses on the shins, blood in the nares and dry blood at the lips, mild bleeding gums when he yawns. Abdomen is soft with no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bone tenderness.

Full blood count: haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4-12), neutrophils 3.6 x10^9/L, lymphocytes 4.0 x10^9/L, platelets 6 x10^9/L (150-400). Film shows large platelets, no blasts. Coagulation profile normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 100/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (110-140), WCC 8.2 x10^9/L (4-12), platelets 6 x10^9/L (150-400), film large platelets no blasts, coags normal
data_table.Exam: petechiae, bruises, active epistaxis, bleeding gums, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with observation only, arrange platelet count in 48 hours, avoid contact sports and NSAIDs
options.rationale: Observation alone applies to dry purpura (skin bruising and petechiae only) in a well child; active mucosal bleeding (wet purpura) shifts management towards pharmacological intervention due to intracranial bleed risk. (Source: RCH ITP)

options.text: Admit and administer intravenous immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg as a single dose with paracetamol pre-medication
options.rationale: Newly diagnosed ITP with wet purpura (mucosal bleeding, epistaxis, gum bleed) plus platelets under 20 x10^9/L warrants urgent platelet elevation; IVIG 0.8 to 1 g/kg gives fastest platelet rise (typically within 24 to 48 h) with a favourable side-effect profile in children. (Source: RCH ITP)

options.text: Transfuse a single unit of pooled platelets to raise the count acutely and prevent further mucosal bleeding
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in ITP is generally ineffective because transfused platelets are destroyed by autoantibody; reserve for life-threatening bleeding as a bridging measure with immunoglobulin and steroid together. (Source: RCH ITP)

options.text: Perform bone marrow aspirate today to exclude leukaemia before commencing any specific therapy for this presentation
options.rationale: Bone marrow aspirate is not required when the presentation is classic ITP (isolated thrombocytopenia, well child, no atypical features on film); it may be done later only if the response to first-line therapy is atypical. (Source: RCH ITP)

options.text: Commence prednisolone 4 mg/kg daily for 4 days without further investigation and review platelet count at day 7
options.rationale: High-dose oral steroid is a valid alternative but is slower to raise platelets than IVIG and requires excluding malignancy on film beforehand; IVIG is preferred in active mucosal bleeding for speed of response. (Source: RCH ITP)

explanation.summary: ITP with wet purpura in a child (active mucosal bleeding) and platelets under 20 x10^9/L is a treatment indication because of the small but serious risk of intracranial haemorrhage. IVIG 0.8 to 1 g/kg is first-line for speed of platelet rise. Dry purpura in a well child with isolated thrombocytopenia may be observed. Bone marrow aspirate is not required if the film is otherwise normal.
key_points: Dry purpura, well child: observe
Wet purpura or platelets <20: treat (IVIG first-line for speed)
Steroid alternative (prednisolone 4 mg/kg/d x 4d) if IVIG contraindicated
Platelet transfusion only for life-threatening bleed as bridge
explanation.pearls: Paediatric ICH risk in ITP is 0.1 to 1%; wet purpura triples risk. Avoid IM injections, NSAIDs, aspirin, and contact sport while count is low.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-year-old girl 6 hours into treatment of new type 1 diabetes with severe diabetic ketoacidosis. On admission her pH was 7.02, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L. She received a 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus and has been on 0.9 percent saline with potassium at maintenance plus 5 percent deficit replacement over 48 hours, with an insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/hour. Her glucose has fallen from 32 to 14 mmol/L. She had been chatty and reading her book.

At this review she complains of a new headache, has vomited once, and is now more drowsy (GCS 12: E3V4M5). Blood pressure has risen from 108/64 to 138/86 and her pulse has fallen from 118 to 68. There is no papilloedema visible but pupils are equal and reactive. Her most recent electrolytes show sodium 138, glucose 12, and pH 7.22.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68 (was 118), blood pressure 138/86 (was 108/64), respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Progress: 6 hours DKA Rx, glucose 32 to 12, pH 7.02 to 7.22
data_table.Neuro: new headache, one vomit, GCS 12 (E3V4M5), pupils equal and reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion to 0.1 unit/kg/hour and add dextrose 10 percent to accelerate resolution of acidosis and ketogenesis
options.rationale: The concern here is cerebral oedema, not persistent acidosis; increasing insulin without addressing the neurological signs is dangerous. Ongoing rehydration and steady insulin at 0.05 unit/kg/hour is appropriate provided glucose fall is not too fast. (Source: RCH DKA)

options.text: Administer another 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus to correct hypovolaemia given her drowsiness and headache
options.rationale: Additional aggressive rehydration risks worsening cerebral oedema; total fluid rate should be reduced by one-third when oedema is suspected. Rising BP and falling pulse are Cushing physiology, not hypovolaemia. (Source: RCH DKA)

options.text: Give 3 percent saline 3 mL/kg over 15 minutes or mannitol 0.5 g/kg, reduce fluid rate by one-third, arrange CT after treatment
options.rationale: Bradycardia and rising BP with headache, vomiting and depressed conscious level are Muir/Glaser cerebral oedema criteria requiring immediate hyperosmolar therapy; 3 percent saline 3 mL/kg IV (or mannitol 0.5 g/kg) is first-line before any imaging. (Source: RCH DKA)

options.text: Arrange an immediate CT head to confirm cerebral oedema before commencing any specific therapy for the neurological deterioration
options.rationale: Treatment must not be delayed for imaging when cerebral oedema is clinically apparent; hyperosmolar therapy is given first, then CT once stabilised (or if there is no response). (Source: RCH DKA)

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV to correct the residual metabolic acidosis and improve cerebral perfusion during recovery
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is contraindicated in paediatric DKA except in life-threatening hyperkalaemia because it worsens cerebral oedema and paradoxical CNS acidosis. (Source: RCH DKA)

explanation.summary: Cerebral oedema is the leading cause of DKA mortality in children. Risk factors include younger age, severe acidosis at presentation, higher urea, low PaCO2, and treatment with bicarbonate or excess fluid. Warning signs (Muir/Glaser): headache, recurrent vomiting, drowsiness, incontinence, hypertension with bradycardia, cranial nerve palsy, abnormal breathing pattern. Treatment is immediate hyperosmolar therapy (3 percent saline 3 mL/kg over 15 minutes or mannitol 0.5 g/kg over 15 minutes), reduce fluid rate, elevate head, and CT after stabilisation.
key_points: Cushing physiology (hypertension + bradycardia) with headache/vomiting equals cerebral oedema
Treat with 3% saline 3 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 g/kg IV before CT
Reduce fluid rate by one-third; avoid rapid glucose fall (>5 mmol/L/h)
Avoid bicarbonate; add dextrose when glucose <14 to prevent hypoglycaemia
explanation.pearls: Fluid deficit calculation in paediatric DKA: assume 5 to 7% dehydration in DKA, 10% in HHS; replace over 48 hours plus maintenance. Two-bag system (0.9% saline vs 0.9% saline plus 10% dextrose) allows steady glucose fall.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-month-old boy who has had a temperature of 39 to 40 degrees Celsius for 6 days. He has been listless, refused feeds intermittently, and had a single loose stool this morning. On examination today: irritable but consolable, a diffuse maculopapular rash across the trunk that has been present 3 days, mild bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, dry cracked lips without oral ulcers, no lymphadenopathy, no peripheral changes. He has not had a coryzal illness. No known unwell contacts.

Bloods: haemoglobin 96 g/L (105-135), white cell count 18.2 x10^9/L (5-15), neutrophils 12.6 x10^9/L, platelets 512 x10^9/L (150-450), CRP 118 mg/L (below 5), ESR 82 mm/h, albumin 24 g/L (35-50), ALT 88 U/L (below 40), sodium 132 mmol/L. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria. Blood cultures at 24 h are negative. Chest X-ray is clear.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 96 g/L, WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, platelets 512 x10^9/L, CRP 118 mg/L (<5), ESR 82 mm/h, albumin 24 g/L (35-50), ALT 88 U/L (<40)
data_table.Urine: sterile pyuria on dipstick and microscopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start high-dose oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for 5 days for a suspected autoimmune inflammatory process while awaiting further tests
options.rationale: Steroids are second-line in Kawasaki (used with IVIG in high-risk or IVIG-resistant cases per the Kobayashi score), not first-line monotherapy; IVIG remains the primary therapy. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

options.text: Continue empirical IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily and repeat sepsis workup at 48 hours if fever persists before considering IVIG
options.rationale: Delaying IVIG beyond day 10 of illness increases coronary artery aneurysm risk; if incomplete Kawasaki criteria are met, treatment should not await further sepsis workup. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol pending viral swab result and community follow-up in 3 to 5 days to reassess response
options.rationale: A well-appearing infant with 6 days of fever and inflammatory picture is unsafe to discharge without excluding Kawasaki disease; missed cases risk coronary aneurysms. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

options.text: Arrange echocardiography now, treat as incomplete Kawasaki disease with IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours and aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg/day
options.rationale: Prolonged fever with only two of five principal Kawasaki criteria (rash and non-purulent conjunctivitis) in an infant with supportive laboratory findings (raised CRP, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, transaminitis, anaemia) meets AHA incomplete Kawasaki criteria; treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, and echocardiography documents coronary status. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

options.text: Add IV vancomycin and admit for observation; hold immunoglobulin until infection is definitely excluded on microbiology
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone are insufficient if incomplete Kawasaki criteria are met and delay definitive therapy; concurrent bacterial infection does not exclude Kawasaki disease. (Source: RCH Kawasaki)

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease diagnosis requires 5 or more days of fever plus 4 of 5 principal criteria (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes, polymorphous rash, peripheral extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy). Incomplete Kawasaki is diagnosed with 2 or 3 principal criteria plus supportive laboratory or echocardiographic findings, particularly in infants under 12 months (highest risk group for coronary aneurysms). Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, with echocardiography to document coronary status.
key_points: Classic KD: fever >=5 days plus 4 of 5 principal criteria
Incomplete KD: fever >=5 days plus 2 or 3 criteria plus supportive labs
Infants <12 months at highest risk for coronary aneurysms; low threshold to treat
Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg single dose + aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg/d (some centres 30 to 80)
explanation.pearls: AHA supportive lab criteria for incomplete KD (at least 3 of): anaemia for age, platelets over 450 after day 7, albumin under 30, ALT elevated, WCC over 15, sterile pyuria. Kobayashi score identifies IVIG-resistant patients for adjunctive steroid.

stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a 60-hour-old term baby born at 39+2 weeks by normal vaginal delivery, birth weight 3.4 kg. Mother has blood group O positive with anti-A antibodies. Baby was noted to be visibly jaundiced by 24 hours of age. He has been feeding briefly but not vigorously, passing 3 wet nappies over the past 12 hours, and lost 6 percent of birth weight.

Baby is now lethargic with a poor cry and reduced tone. Cephalocaudal jaundice extends to soles of feet. He is afebrile, saturating well in air, no bruising, no cephalohaematoma. There is no organomegaly. Bilirubin at admission was 340 micromol/L, now at 60 hours it is 512 micromol/L. Direct antiglobulin test is positive. Baby's blood group is A positive. Reticulocyte count is 8 percent (0.5 to 2). Haemoglobin 128 g/L (145 to 225 at 24 hours). He is on triple-bank intensive phototherapy for the past 4 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 158, blood pressure 62/38, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: total bilirubin 512 umol/L (age 60h phototherapy line ~380, exchange line ~430), DAT positive, retic 8%, Hb 128 g/L, ABO incompatibility
data_table.Rx so far: triple bank intensive phototherapy 4 hours, IV fluids commenced

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue intensive phototherapy alone and repeat serum bilirubin in 6 hours before deciding on exchange transfusion
options.rationale: Bilirubin above the exchange transfusion threshold at 60 hours with clinical features of acute bilirubin encephalopathy (lethargy, poor tone, poor cry) mandates immediate exchange, not further observation on phototherapy alone. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Stop phototherapy to prevent riboflavin depletion and give oral ursodeoxycholic acid 20 mg/kg/day until bilirubin falls
options.rationale: Stopping phototherapy allows further bilirubin rise; ursodeoxycholic acid has no role in unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Continued intensive phototherapy alongside exchange is standard. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Give a top-up transfusion of packed red cells 10 mL/kg to correct the anaemia, then observe with phototherapy for 12 hours
options.rationale: Simple top-up transfusion does not remove circulating bilirubin or antibody; only exchange transfusion clears both and is required at this bilirubin level with encephalopathy. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Administer intravenous phenobarbitone 15 mg/kg loading dose to induce hepatic conjugation of unconjugated bilirubin
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone has a slow onset (days) and no role in acute severe hyperbilirubinaemia with encephalopathy; immediate mechanical clearance by exchange is required. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

options.text: Prepare for double-volume exchange transfusion urgently while continuing intensive phototherapy and giving IVIG 0.5 g/kg for immune haemolysis
options.rationale: Bilirubin over the exchange line at 60 hours with signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy in a baby with immune haemolysis requires urgent double-volume exchange transfusion; IVIG 0.5 g/kg over 2 hours may reduce need for exchange in immune haemolytic disease. (Source: RCH Neonatal Jaundice)

explanation.summary: Severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia with acute bilirubin encephalopathy is a neurological emergency. Immune haemolytic causes (Rh, ABO, minor blood group incompatibility) have a positive DAT and elevated reticulocyte count. When bilirubin exceeds the exchange transfusion threshold on the age-specific nomogram, or when signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy appear (lethargy, hypotonia, poor feed, high-pitched cry, opisthotonos, seizures), immediate double-volume exchange transfusion is indicated with concurrent intensive phototherapy. IVIG 0.5 g/kg reduces need for exchange in immune haemolysis.
key_points: Bilirubin above exchange line OR any acute encephalopathy signs equals immediate exchange
IVIG 0.5 g/kg over 2 hours in immune haemolysis may reduce need for exchange
Continue intensive phototherapy throughout
Isovolumetric exchange with double blood volume (~160 mL/kg)
explanation.pearls: NICE and RCH nomograms differ slightly; the current RCH exchange line at 60 hours for a well term baby is roughly 430 micromol/L (lower with haemolysis or prematurity). Escalate immediately if encephalopathy signs present regardless of exact number.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-year-old girl who presented three weeks ago with palpable purpura over her buttocks and lower limbs, symmetrical ankle and knee joint swelling, and colicky abdominal pain. She was diagnosed with IgA vasculitis (previously called Henoch-Schonlein purpura). Her purpura and abdominal pain resolved with paracetamol; joint swelling settled.

Weekly urinalysis for surveillance now shows blood 3+ and protein 3+. Her spot urine protein/creatinine ratio is 320 mg/mmol (below 20). Serum albumin is 24 g/L (35 to 50), creatinine 78 umol/L (30 to 60 for her age), estimated GFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure is 132/86 which is above the 95th centile for age, sex, and height. She has periorbital and pretibial oedema. Complement C3 and C4 are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 132/86 (>95th centile), respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 78 umol/L (30-60), eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m2, albumin 24 g/L (35-50), C3 normal, C4 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric nephrology urgently and arrange renal biopsy plus commence oral prednisolone pending histology and steroid-based induction
options.rationale: IgA vasculitis nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension and reduced eGFR requires urgent nephrology referral, renal biopsy for prognostic and treatment classification (Oxford/ISKDC), and empirical steroid therapy is often started pending biopsy result. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

options.text: Continue weekly urine surveillance for another 6 months and reassess if proteinuria persists or worsens further
options.rationale: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with reduced GFR and hypertension in IgA vasculitis nephritis requires renal biopsy and specialist input, not further observation which risks progression. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg 8-hourly empirically for possible post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis pending ASOT results
options.rationale: Normal complement and preceding IgA vasculitis do not fit post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis; antibiotics are not indicated and delay appropriate immunosuppression assessment. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

options.text: Restrict dietary salt and fluid and reassess urinalysis and blood pressure in 4 weeks at the local GP surgery for review
options.rationale: Dietary measures alone are insufficient for nephritic-nephrotic syndrome with rising creatinine; specialist assessment and biopsy are needed within days, not weeks. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

options.text: Commence enalapril 0.1 mg/kg daily for the hypertension and continue outpatient monitoring monthly without further investigation
options.rationale: ACE inhibitor is a reasonable adjunct but insufficient alone with nephrotic range proteinuria and reduced GFR; biopsy and immunosuppression assessment are the priority. (Source: RCH IgA Vasculitis)

explanation.summary: IgA vasculitis nephritis presents as haematuria and/or proteinuria in the weeks to months after the acute vasculitic illness. Weekly urinalysis for 6 to 12 months detects it early. Indications for renal biopsy and nephrology referral include nephrotic range proteinuria (uPCR over 200 mg/mmol), impaired renal function, persistent hypertension, or persistent macroscopic haematuria and proteinuria beyond 3 months. Steroid-based induction is standard for significant nephritis, guided by biopsy histology.
key_points: Weekly urinalysis for 6 to 12 months after acute IgA vasculitis
Biopsy triggers: nephrotic proteinuria, reduced GFR, hypertension, persistent haematuria+proteinuria
Empiric steroids often started pending biopsy
Preventive steroids do NOT prevent nephritis (KIGARI trial)
explanation.pearls: ISKDC classification I to VI grades severity by crescents; over 50% crescents or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis has worse prognosis. Renal outcomes are the main long-term determinant, with 1 to 5% risk of ESKD in nephritic cases.

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to ED for a 3-year-old boy with 4 days of fever, sore throat, and increasing neck stiffness. Today he has developed drooling, refuses to swallow, and holds his neck extended. He is anxious, sits upright on his father's lap, muffled voice, mild stridor at rest, no drooling on arrival. Temperature 39.4, pulse 148, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 96 percent on room air.

He will not open his mouth for examination. There is a visible swelling in the posterior pharyngeal wall on limited view. There is tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Bloods: WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 186 mg/L. Neck lateral X-ray shows widening of the prevertebral soft tissues at C3 to 5 to greater than half the vertebral body width. Blood cultures have been taken.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Exam: sits upright, muffled voice, mild stridor, neck extended, will not open mouth, tender cervical nodes
data_table.Bloods and imaging: WCC 22 x10^9/L, CRP 186 mg/L (<5), lateral neck XR prevertebral soft tissue widening C3-5

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Perform bedside incision and drainage with local anaesthesia in ED before transfer to reduce ongoing airway swelling and time to source control
options.rationale: Bedside drainage of a paediatric retropharyngeal abscess risks catastrophic airway loss and aspiration; drainage is done in theatre with definitive airway. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

options.text: Cannulate immediately in ED, take blood cultures, and give IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and metronidazole 15 mg/kg before ENT is contacted
options.rationale: Cannulation may cause the child to cry and lose the airway; treatment in a compromised paediatric airway starts with keeping the child calm and moving to a controlled theatre environment, then antibiotics and drainage. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

options.text: Keep child calm, call ENT and paediatric anaesthetics urgently, transfer to theatre for controlled inhalational induction and drainage
options.rationale: Retropharyngeal abscess with airway compromise (stridor, muffled voice, drooling, opisthotonos) in a young child requires controlled airway management in theatre with senior ENT and paediatric anaesthetics; distress can precipitate obstruction. Drainage and IV antibiotics follow airway control. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

options.text: Nebulise adrenaline 5 mg and give IV dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg for stridor, then arrange contrast CT neck once he settles
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone are for croup, not deep neck space infection; CT is helpful but only after airway assessment in theatre because a child with mild stridor at rest can decompensate on scanner. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

options.text: Perform urgent rapid sequence intubation in the ED using ketamine and rocuronium to secure the airway then arrange transfer
options.rationale: Emergency intubation of a paediatric distorted airway in ED risks catastrophic failure; the standard is inhalational induction in theatre by paediatric anaesthetics with ENT available for surgical airway backup. (Source: RCH Retropharyngeal Abscess)

explanation.summary: Retropharyngeal abscess presents in toddlers as fever, sore throat, drooling, muffled voice, neck extension or torticollis, with lateral neck film showing prevertebral widening (over half vertebral body width at C2, over one vertebral body at C6). Management prioritises airway: keep the child calm, escalate to paediatric anaesthetics and ENT, controlled inhalational induction in theatre, then drainage and IV antibiotics.
key_points: Airway first: keep calm, do not agitate, escalate to ENT and paediatric anaesthetics
Controlled inhalational induction in theatre, NOT RSI in ED
Empiric IV ceftriaxone plus clindamycin (or metronidazole) after airway secured
Contrast CT for surgical planning after airway assessment
explanation.pearls: Distinguish from epiglottitis (rapid onset, tripod, drooling, no torticollis) and croup (barking cough, no drooling). Retropharyngeal lateral film sign: prevertebral soft tissue >7 mm at C2 or >14 mm at C6 (or >1x vertebral body width).

stem:
You are the consultation-liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman with a 12-year history of bipolar I disorder on lithium and quetiapine, admitted to the medical ward 3 days ago after her family found her mute in bed. She has stopped eating and drinking, is refusing medication, and has been withdrawn from the community mental health service for two months.

On examination she is awake with eyes open, staring past you, not responsive to questioning. When you raise her right arm above her head it remains suspended for over 60 seconds. She exhibits echopraxia when you touch your nose. When you attempt to move her limb she resists with equal counter-force in both directions. She has been afebrile, saturations normal, blood pressure 128/78, pulse 92. Bloods including CK, TFTs, calcium, and infection screen are normal. Head CT is unremarkable. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale score is 18.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: CK 148 U/L (<170), TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), infection screen negative, head CT unremarkable
data_table.Exam: mute, waxy flexibility, echopraxia, gegenhalten, BFCRS 18

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological step?

options.text: Give IM haloperidol 5 mg to sedate her and enable enteral feeding via nasogastric tube for adequate hydration
options.rationale: Haloperidol worsens catatonia and increases risk of NMS; it should be avoided in favour of benzodiazepine trial as the diagnostic and therapeutic step. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Continue current quetiapine and start olanzapine 10 mg for suspected relapse of bipolar affective disorder with psychosis
options.rationale: Antipsychotic monotherapy can worsen catatonia and precipitate malignant catatonia or neuroleptic malignant syndrome; benzodiazepines are first-line, with antipsychotics deferred until catatonia resolves. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Commence electroconvulsive therapy immediately without first trialling any benzodiazepine treatment for this presentation
options.rationale: ECT is second-line after benzodiazepine trial (or first-line in malignant catatonia); a lorazepam challenge is the standard first step in non-malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Give IV lorazepam 2 mg as a challenge and observe for symptomatic response over 5 to 10 minutes
options.rationale: Catatonia (BFCRS 18) is confirmed on positive lorazepam challenge with a benzodiazepine trial; 1 to 2 mg IV lorazepam produces symptomatic relief in 60 to 80 percent of cases within 10 minutes and both diagnoses and initiates ongoing therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

options.text: Start amantadine 100 mg 12-hourly for NMDA-glutamate modulation as first-line therapy for treatment-refractory catatonia today
options.rationale: Amantadine and NMDA-modulating agents are reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory catatonia; the first-line remains benzodiazepine trial before escalation. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome with motor, behavioural, and autonomic features. DSM-5 requires 3 or more of 12 features including catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, stupor, agitation, posturing, mannerisms, stereotypies, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia, and negativism. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale of 3 or more items or 6 or more total suggests catatonia. Lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV or IM) is diagnostic and therapeutic in 60 to 80 percent of cases. Malignant catatonia (autonomic instability, hyperthermia) is a life-threatening variant requiring ECT.
key_points: First-line: lorazepam challenge 1 to 2 mg IV or IM
Continue lorazepam 4 to 8 mg daily divided if responsive
Second-line: ECT (first-line if malignant catatonia)
Avoid antipsychotics until resolved (risk of NMS)
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia clues: fever above 38 C, autonomic instability, elevated CK, rhabdomyolysis; treat as NMS with immediate ECT while withholding antipsychotics. Overlap with NMS is significant; clinical picture often decides.

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome in anorexia nervosa admission
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old woman referred from the eating disorders clinic. She has a 4-year history of anorexia nervosa (restrictive subtype) and has lost 8 kg over 2 months. Current BMI is 12.8 (weight 34 kg, height 163 cm). She is bradycardic at 42, blood pressure 88/54 lying and 74/48 standing, temperature 35.4, ECG shows sinus bradycardia with corrected QT of 460 ms and prominent U waves.

Admission bloods: sodium 138, potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70 to 1.10), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.50), glucose 3.2 mmol/L, albumin 34 g/L, creatinine 42 umol/L, calcium 2.20 mmol/L, LFTs mildly deranged with ALT 68 U/L.

The medical team has been asked to plan refeeding. She has been eating minimal food for two weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 42, blood pressure 88/54 lying and 74/48 standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 35.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), glucose 3.2 mmol/L, ALT 68 U/L
data_table.ECG: sinus bradycardia 42, QTc 460 ms, prominent U waves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate refeeding plan?

options.text: Withhold all nutrition for 48 hours to allow gradual electrolyte normalisation then start at 15 kcal/kg/day with oral supplements once stable
options.rationale: Prolonged starvation while inpatient worsens outcomes; the correct approach is early low-energy refeeding with concurrent electrolyte and thiamine cover, not further fasting. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Commence a standard maintenance diet at 30 kcal/kg/day today with oral supplementation and correct electrolytes only if levels fall further
options.rationale: Full maintenance energy in a very high refeeding risk patient causes acute refeeding syndrome (cardiac failure, arrhythmia, Wernicke encephalopathy); start slow and correct pre-emptively. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and deliver 100 percent of estimated caloric needs immediately by continuous feed to accelerate weight restoration
options.rationale: Continuous full-target NG feeding in severe undernutrition precipitates refeeding syndrome; NG feeding is used when oral intake is inadequate but starts at low energy with slow escalation. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Give a rapid IV glucose bolus of 200 mL 10 percent dextrose to correct hypoglycaemia, then start standard diet at full maintenance today
options.rationale: IV glucose without thiamine cover risks Wernicke encephalopathy; hypoglycaemia in anorexia is corrected with oral or small enteral carbohydrate after thiamine, not rapid IV boluses in a stable patient. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

options.text: Start oral thiamine 200 mg daily, correct electrolyte deficits first, then commence energy at 20 kcal/kg/day and increase over 5 to 7 days
options.rationale: Severe anorexia (BMI 12.8) with hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypophosphataemia is at very high refeeding risk; start thiamine BEFORE any carbohydrate, replace electrolytes, then commence low energy (10 to 20 kcal/kg/day) with slow uptitration and daily electrolyte monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is triggered by carbohydrate reintroduction after starvation, driving insulin release and rapid intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, causing arrhythmia, cardiac failure, Wernicke encephalopathy, and death. Very high risk criteria (NICE): BMI under 14, minimal intake over 15 days, weight loss over 20 percent, or existing hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia or hypophosphataemia. Start thiamine before glucose, replace electrolytes pre-emptively, start energy low (10 to 20 kcal/kg/day) with slow escalation and daily monitoring.
key_points: Thiamine 200 to 300 mg PO daily BEFORE any carbohydrate
Correct K, Mg, PO4 pre-emptively and daily
Start energy at 10 to 20 kcal/kg/day, uptitrate over 5 to 7 days
Cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia in first week
explanation.pearls: MARSIPAN/AN-CHECK Australian criteria for medical admission: BMI <13, pulse <40, systolic BP <80, postural drop >20 mmHg, temperature <35.5 C, potassium <3.0. Any one is grounds for medical stabilisation.

subtopic_detail: Acute-on-chronic lithium toxicity with renal impairment
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 62-year-old woman with a 25-year history of bipolar I on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for maintenance. She started ramipril 10 mg for hypertension 3 weeks ago and had a gastroenteritis 4 days ago. Her family brought her in because she has been increasingly confused, tremulous, and unsteady over 48 hours. On examination she is drowsy (GCS 12), coarse tremor of both hands, hyperreflexia, myoclonic jerks, ataxia. She is not febrile.

Bloods: lithium level 3.4 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6 to 1.0), sodium 148 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, urea 14 mmol/L, creatinine 216 umol/L (baseline 78 six months ago), eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. TFTs normal. Anion gap normal. ECG shows sinus rhythm at 92 with T-wave flattening and one PVC per 10 beats.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: lithium 3.4 mmol/L (0.6-1.0 therapeutic), sodium 148 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 216 umol/L (baseline 78), eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2
data_table.Neuro: GCS 12, coarse tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, ataxia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold lithium, commence IV 0.9 percent saline at maintenance plus 5 percent deficit, and refer to renal for urgent haemodialysis
options.rationale: Lithium above 2.5 mmol/L with severe neurological features (altered consciousness, myoclonus, ataxia) or above 4.0 mmol/L regardless of symptoms, especially with renal impairment reducing excretion, is an indication for haemodialysis. Withhold lithium and provide IV saline while dialysis is arranged. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Give IV activated charcoal 50 g nasogastrically to reduce further lithium absorption before further specific management
options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium (it is an ionic salt with poor charcoal affinity) and is contraindicated in reduced GCS without a secure airway; dialysis is the correct removal method. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence forced alkaline diuresis with intravenous sodium bicarbonate to accelerate renal lithium clearance
options.rationale: Forced alkaline diuresis is not the treatment for lithium toxicity; lithium is not weak-acid protein-bound. IV saline is used to restore volume and improve excretion, and haemodialysis is required in severe cases. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue lithium at a reduced dose of 250 mg nocte and add oral quetiapine 50 mg for symptomatic control while awaiting stabilisation
options.rationale: Continuing lithium in severe toxicity with renal impairment is dangerous; complete withdrawal until level and renal function normalise is required. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Give intravenous physostigmine 2 mg to reverse the anticholinergic effects contributing to her acute confusional state
options.rationale: Lithium toxicity is not anticholinergic; physostigmine has no role and may cause bradyarrhythmia and seizure. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity is precipitated by dehydration, renal impairment, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides, NSAIDs, or dose error. Severity is not solely by level: chronic toxicity may have neurological features at lower levels than acute overdose. Indications for haemodialysis (EXTRIP criteria): level over 4.0 mmol/L regardless of symptoms, level over 2.5 mmol/L with severe neurological features or renal impairment, or level over 2.5 with expected clearance time above 36 hours. Withhold lithium, IV saline for volume, seizure precautions, and refer to renal.
key_points: Withhold lithium; IV 0.9% saline to restore volume
Haemodialysis indicated: level >4.0, or >2.5 with severe symptoms or renal impairment
Charcoal does NOT bind lithium; not indicated
Screen for ACEi/ARB/thiazide/NSAID interaction
explanation.pearls: EXTRIP working group thresholds are widely adopted. Rebound rise after dialysis is common due to redistribution; monitor 6- to 12-hourly levels and repeat dialysis if rebound >1.0 with symptoms.

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on-call reviewing a 42-year-old man admitted 48 hours ago after presenting acutely psychotic and agitated. He was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg BD and lorazepam 2 mg TDS. He has a background of major depressive disorder for which he takes citalopram 40 mg, and his GP added tramadol 100 mg TDS two weeks ago for back pain. Overnight he became increasingly restless, developed generalised tremor, and vomited twice.

On examination: temperature 38.6, pulse 128, blood pressure 168/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96 percent on room air. He is alert and oriented but confused. Pupils are 6 mm, reactive. Marked lower-limb hyperreflexia with inducible ankle clonus (6 beats) and spontaneous myoclonic jerks. Increased tone in the legs more than the arms. Bowel sounds hyperactive. Diaphoretic. CK 220 U/L (below 170).

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 168/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: CK 220 U/L (<170), WCC 10.4 x10^9/L, creatinine 84 umol/L, lithium not applicable
data_table.Neuro: 6 mm reactive pupils, lower limb hyperreflexia > upper, inducible ankle clonus 6 beats, myoclonic jerks, diaphoresis, hyperactive bowel sounds

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; stop olanzapine, commence dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV and bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally
options.rationale: NMS is characterised by lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, sluggish pupils, bradykinesia, marked CK rise, and normal or reduced bowel sounds; the picture here (lower limb hyperreflexia, clonus, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds, mild CK rise) is classic serotonin syndrome. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Serotonin syndrome; cease citalopram and tramadol, provide supportive care with IV fluids and benzodiazepines, add cyproheptadine 12 mg orally if severe
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria: use of serotonergic agent plus spontaneous or inducible clonus with agitation, diaphoresis or hyperthermia, or ocular clonus) here from citalopram plus tramadol combination; treat by ceasing serotonergic agents, aggressive supportive care with benzodiazepines and fluids, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally in moderate to severe cases. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Anticholinergic toxidrome; give physostigmine 2 mg IV and monitor cardiac rhythm continuously until symptoms resolve
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxidrome causes dry skin, mydriasis, absent bowel sounds, and urinary retention; diaphoresis and hyperactive bowel sounds argue against and physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Sympathomimetic toxidrome from illicit stimulant use; administer IV benzodiazepines only and observe for clinical improvement
options.rationale: Sympathomimetic (cocaine, methamphetamine) toxidrome shares hyperthermia and hypertension but does not cause clonus and lower-limb-predominant hyperreflexia; the temporal association with citalopram and tramadol makes serotonin syndrome the diagnosis. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

options.text: Malignant hyperthermia; give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV every 5 minutes and active surface cooling with ice packs and fanning
options.rationale: Malignant hyperthermia is an anaesthetic emergency triggered by volatile agents or succinylcholine, with masseter spasm and severe hyperthermia; it does not fit this clinical picture with no anaesthesia exposure. (Source: eTG Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome and NMS can look similar but differ in key ways. Serotonin syndrome (SS): rapid onset after adding or increasing a serotonergic agent, lower limb hyperreflexia with clonus (spontaneous or inducible), mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds, diaphoresis, and mild-moderate CK rise. NMS: subacute (24 to 72 h), lead-pipe rigidity throughout, hyporeflexia, sluggish pupils, absent bowel sounds, marked CK rise (often over 1000). Treatment: cease offending drug; SS uses benzodiazepines and cyproheptadine; NMS uses dantrolene and bromocriptine.
key_points: SS: clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, hyperactive gut, sweaty, mild CK rise
NMS: rigid, hyporeflexic, sluggish pupils, absent gut, high CK
SS treatment: cease drug, IV fluids, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine 12 mg PO for moderate/severe
NMS treatment: cease drug, IV fluids, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg, bromocriptine 2.5 mg PO
explanation.pearls: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria: use of serotonergic agent plus 1 of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; tremor and hyperreflexia; hypertonia + temp >38 C + ocular or inducible clonus.

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on-call in ED reviewing a 27-year-old woman brought by ambulance after making superficial parallel cuts to her left forearm. She has known borderline personality disorder, is engaged with a public mental health service where she attends weekly DBT skills group and monthly psychiatrist review. She has 14 prior admissions for self-harm and one prior serious attempt with paracetamol overdose 3 years ago. Tonight she cut after an argument with her partner. She has not consumed alcohol or drugs.

On assessment she is calm, engaged, and future-oriented. She apologises for coming in and says she used all her DBT skills first, only cut after they failed. She wants to go home. She has no active plan, has removed the razor blades from her flat, has agreed to phone her case manager tomorrow morning, and will attend group later this week. Her partner is present, supportive, and can stay with her overnight. Wounds do not require sutures.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Assessment: calm, engaged, apologetic, future-oriented, denies active plan, DBT-engaged, safety plan in place, partner supportive
data_table.Wound: 3 superficial parallel forearm cuts, no bleeding, dressed, no suture needed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act to a psychiatric ward for observation given the pattern of repeated self-harm
options.rationale: Involuntary admission for chronic self-harm in stable BPD is generally harmful (institutional dependency, reinforcement of admission-as-solution) and does not meet MHA criteria when there is engagement, no active intent, and adequate community support. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Refer for a 6 to 8 week course of ECT to reduce her recurrent affective dysregulation and self-harm behaviours
options.rationale: ECT has no role in BPD unless there is a co-occurring severe treatment-resistant major depressive episode; it is not indicated for the personality disorder itself. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Admit voluntarily to a psychiatric ward for a 3 to 5 day break and commence olanzapine 5 mg for affective instability during admission
options.rationale: Brief admissions for BPD are unhelpful and pharmacotherapy adds side effects without evidence of benefit; medication targets specific comorbidities, not the personality diagnosis itself. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Discharge with a joint written safety plan, contact her case manager tomorrow, and arrange next scheduled DBT session as planned this week
options.rationale: Chronic BPD self-harm without acute imminent risk is best managed in the community with existing supports; admission is not therapeutic for chronic suicidality and disrupts the DBT frame. Discharge with a documented safety plan, early follow-up, and use of established supports is the evidence-based approach. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

options.text: Prescribe short-course diazepam 5 mg TDS for 2 weeks and increase her SSRI dose empirically to reduce chronic self-harm behaviour
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are contraindicated in BPD (worsen disinhibition and impulsive self-harm); SSRI titration for BPD chronic self-harm is not evidence-based unless treating a defined depressive episode. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)

explanation.summary: Chronic self-harm in stable BPD is best managed in the community with an existing therapeutic frame (DBT, MBT, or schema therapy). Admission does not reduce long-term suicide risk and often reinforces admission-as-coping. Discharge is appropriate when the patient is future-oriented, has engaged with skills first, has means restriction, has follow-up scheduled, and has social support. Admission is reserved for co-occurring acute severe MDD, acute psychosis, acute intoxication, or a clear change in trajectory suggesting shift to imminent lethality.
key_points: Chronic self-harm in stable BPD: community management with safety plan
Admission indications: acute severe MDD, psychosis, intoxication, clear escalation
Avoid benzodiazepines (disinhibition), pharmacotherapy targets comorbidity
Structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, SFT, TFT) is first-line
explanation.pearls: Australian NHMRC BPD guideline (2013, still current) emphasises psychological therapies as primary treatment; medication only for specific comorbid mood or psychotic symptoms. Admissions if used should be brief and goal-focused.

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder (diagnosed at 22, 3 prior manic episodes, 4 prior depressive episodes) currently in a 5-week depressive episode. She has low mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia (sleeping 12 to 14 hours), psychomotor slowing, guilt, poor concentration, and passive suicidal thoughts without plan. She stopped lithium 4 months ago because she disliked hand tremor and lost weight. She has never taken an antidepressant.

Her weight is 68 kg, BMI 24. Thyroid function normal, U&Es normal (eGFR over 90), creatinine 62 umol/L. Her most recent manic episode was 3 years ago on lithium monotherapy at level 0.6 mmol/L; she was hospitalised for two weeks. She and her husband are planning a pregnancy in the next 12 to 18 months.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: TSH 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine 62 umol/L, eGFR >90, calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), pregnancy test negative
data_table.History: bipolar I, 3 manic and 4 depressive episodes, off lithium 4 months, planning pregnancy 12-18 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy for this depressive episode?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg nocte plus fluoxetine 20 mg daily (OFC combination) as first-line for the current bipolar depressive episode
options.rationale: OFC is effective for bipolar depression but not first-line preferred in pregnancy planning due to metabolic and teratogenic concerns; lithium or lamotrigine are preferred initial choices with clear prior response. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg alone with no mood stabiliser cover because the priority is treating the acute depressive episode symptomatically
options.rationale: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar I depression risks switch to mania and rapid cycling; mood stabiliser cover is required if any antidepressant is used, and antidepressant use in bipolar I is limited. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Commence sodium valproate 500 mg BD as monotherapy for both mood stabilisation and treatment of the depressive episode she now has
options.rationale: Valproate is highly teratogenic (neural tube defects, autism spectrum, IQ reduction) and is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy under the pregnancy prevention programme; not appropriate here. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Commence carbamazepine 200 mg BD as first-line mood stabiliser and add fluoxetine 20 mg for the current depressive symptomatology
options.rationale: Carbamazepine is second-line for bipolar and is a teratogen (neural tube defects, oral clefts) requiring reliable contraception; fluoxetine monotherapy risks manic switch. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

options.text: Restart lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte alone, target level 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L, and involve reproductive psychiatry for pregnancy planning
options.rationale: Lithium is a first-line treatment for bipolar depression with strong evidence for both depression and prophylaxis and prior demonstrated response; her prior tremor and weight loss are manageable. Preconception counselling weighs cardiac malformation risk (Ebstein anomaly ~1 in 1000 to 2000) versus recurrence risk in pregnancy. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar)

explanation.summary: First-line options for bipolar I depression include lithium, quetiapine, and lamotrigine (slower onset), each with evidence and specific considerations. Lithium suits a patient with prior response, adequate renal function, and long-term prophylactic need, with the pregnancy-planning discussion including Ebstein anomaly risk (~1 in 1000 to 2000 with first trimester exposure) versus untreated bipolar recurrence risk (approximately 50 percent in pregnancy and postpartum). Antidepressant monotherapy is avoided in bipolar I because of the switch risk.
key_points: First-line for bipolar depression: lithium, quetiapine, lamotrigine
Avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar I (switch to mania)
Valproate contraindicated in women of reproductive age unless in PPP
Preconception counselling: risk of untreated illness vs teratogenicity
explanation.pearls: CANMAT 2018 first-line for bipolar I depression: quetiapine, lurasidone, lithium, lamotrigine, and lithium/lamotrigine combined; olanzapine-fluoxetine second-line. Ebstein anomaly risk with first trimester lithium ~1 in 1000 to 2000, up from baseline 1 in 20000.

subtopic_detail: Chronic functional constipation with faecal impaction
stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-year-old boy in clinic with an 18-month history of infrequent hard stools (1 to 2 per week), painful defaecation, stool withholding behaviour, and 4 months of daily faecal soiling. His parents describe him passing large stools that block the toilet. He has been drinking adequate fluids, has a varied diet, and has no red flags on history (no delayed meconium, no bilious vomiting, no failure to thrive, normal spine and back examination, normal anal position).

On examination he is well grown at 50th centile for weight and height, abdomen is soft with a large firm mass in the left lower quadrant, no visible pelvic organs. Anal inspection is normal, no anal tags or fissures. His parents have tried lactulose, senna, and dietary fibre without meaningful improvement over 3 months.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 96/60, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Exam: large firm faecal mass LLQ, normal spine, normal anal position, no fissure or tag
data_table.History: 18-month course, hard weekly stools, withholding, 4 months daily soiling, prior lactulose and senna failed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Commence high-dose oral macrogol (PEG) for 3 days for faecal disimpaction, then maintenance macrogol titrated to soft daily stools
options.rationale: Chronic functional constipation with faecal impaction requires disimpaction with high-dose oral macrogol (1 to 1.5 g/kg/day for 3 days) then maintenance dosing titrated to soft daily stools; parent education and behavioural toileting are essential adjuncts. (Source: RCH Constipation)

options.text: Perform a rectal biopsy urgently to exclude Hirschsprung disease before commencing any further laxative therapy for this child
options.rationale: Hirschsprung disease presents in early infancy with delayed meconium and typically failure to thrive; a well-grown 5-year-old with classic functional constipation history does not warrant biopsy. (Source: RCH Constipation)

options.text: Perform daily bisacodyl suppositories at home for two weeks followed by oral senna as long-term maintenance therapy for this child
options.rationale: Rectal treatments are more distressing for children and less effective than oral macrogol for both disimpaction and maintenance; oral therapy is first-line unless oral is not tolerated. (Source: RCH Constipation)

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for an ACE (antegrade continence enema) procedure given his failure of prior conservative therapy over months
options.rationale: ACE is reserved for refractory constipation after optimised medical therapy including adequate disimpaction and maintenance macrogol with behavioural support has failed. (Source: RCH Constipation)

options.text: Prescribe a lactose-free diet trial for 4 weeks with reassessment because cow milk protein allergy is a leading cause of functional constipation
options.rationale: Cow milk protein allergy contributes in a small subset (particularly infants) but is not the first-line intervention in a 5-year-old with classic functional constipation; disimpaction and maintenance is standard. (Source: RCH Constipation)

explanation.summary: Chronic functional constipation with faecal impaction in children is managed by (1) disimpaction with high-dose oral macrogol (PEG) for 3 to 7 days, (2) maintenance macrogol titrated to soft daily stools continued for at least 2 to 6 months, (3) toileting behavioural strategy (sit after meals, footstool, reward chart), and (4) parent education. Red flags requiring further workup include delayed meconium, failure to thrive, abnormal spine or perianal examination, or onset before 1 month of age.
key_points: Disimpaction: macrogol 1 to 1.5 g/kg/day PO for 3 days (some centres up to 7)
Maintenance: macrogol titrated to soft daily stool for months, not weeks
Toilet behavioural strategy is essential alongside laxatives
Rectal treatments only if oral fails or refused
explanation.pearls: Movicol Junior (macrogol) sachets: 1 to 2 sachets/day maintenance; 4 to 12 sachets/day for disimpaction depending on age. Do not stop maintenance for at least 2 months of regular painless stools then wean slowly to avoid relapse.

subtopic_detail: Acute gout flare in a patient with chronic kidney disease
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 68-year-old man in the acute medical clinic with 24 hours of a very painful, red, swollen right first metatarsophalangeal joint. He has had two similar episodes previously that self-resolved with paracetamol over 5 to 7 days. He has stage 4 CKD with eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m2 (baseline 22 to 26), hypertension on amlodipine, ischaemic heart disease on aspirin, and takes no other regular medications. He is not on urate-lowering therapy.

On examination the right first MTP joint is warm, tender, erythematous with overlying skin taut and shiny, and range of motion is severely restricted by pain. There is a small tophaceous nodule on the right olecranon. He is afebrile, blood pressure 132/78, pulse 88. Serum urate today is 0.52 mmol/L (upper limit 0.42), creatinine 236 umol/L, CRP 68 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 236 umol/L (baseline 220-240), eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m2, urate 0.52 mmol/L (<0.42), CRP 68 mg/L (<5)
data_table.Exam: right first MTP joint warm, erythematous, swollen, tender, right olecranon tophus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line therapy for the acute flare?

options.text: Commence oral naproxen 500 mg BD for 5 days with a proton pump inhibitor for gastroprotection during acute treatment
options.rationale: NSAIDs are contraindicated in stage 4 CKD because of the risk of further renal impairment and hyperkalaemia; steroids or intra-articular therapy are safer alternatives. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for 5 days and discuss commencing allopurinol at low dose after the acute flare has resolved
options.rationale: In stage 4 CKD, NSAIDs are contraindicated and colchicine risks accumulation and toxicity; oral prednisolone 25 to 30 mg daily for 3 to 5 days is a preferred first-line acute anti-inflammatory choice in CKD. Urate-lowering therapy is discussed after the acute flare with allopurinol started low and titrated. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence oral colchicine 1 mg then 500 micrograms 1 hour later, then 500 micrograms 12-hourly for a full 3 days
options.rationale: Colchicine accumulates in stage 4 CKD (eGFR under 30) with high toxicity risk (neuromyopathy, cytopenias); dose reduction to 500 micrograms daily is possible but steroid is generally preferred. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence allopurinol 300 mg daily now to reduce serum urate and treat the acute flare simultaneously in one visit
options.rationale: Starting allopurinol during an acute flare can prolong or worsen it; also 300 mg is too high a start dose in stage 4 CKD (start 50 mg and titrate). Urate-lowering therapy is discussed after the flare settles. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

options.text: Perform bedside joint aspiration for intra-articular corticosteroid injection and send synovial fluid for gram stain and crystals
options.rationale: Intra-articular steroid is reasonable for a single joint when infection is excluded, but oral prednisolone is simpler and equally effective in this context; aspirating a first MTP is technically difficult and injection risks contamination. (Source: eTG Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Acute gout in CKD is treated with oral or intra-articular corticosteroid as first-line because NSAIDs are contraindicated and colchicine accumulates. Oral prednisolone 25 to 30 mg for 3 to 5 days is effective and generally well tolerated. Urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol) is initiated after the acute flare settles, starting at low dose (50 mg in eGFR under 30) and uptitrated to a serum urate target of 0.36 mmol/L (or 0.30 with tophi), with colchicine or NSAID cover as flare prophylaxis where safe.
key_points: NSAIDs contraindicated in CKD; colchicine accumulates in eGFR <30
Oral prednisolone 25 to 30 mg for 3 to 5 days is first-line in CKD
Allopurinol start dose in eGFR <30: 50 mg, titrate every 4 weeks
Target serum urate <0.36 mmol/L (<0.30 with tophi)
explanation.pearls: HLA-B*5801 screening pre-allopurinol reduces SJS/TEN risk (particularly Han Chinese, Korean, Thai populations). Febuxostat is an alternative XO inhibitor but has cardiovascular safety concerns and is second-line.

stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 32-year-old primiparous woman at her routine 6-week postnatal check. Her baby is thriving and exclusively breastfed. She scored 15 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) today (positive 13 or above), scoring 1 on item 10 (thought of harming self). She reports 4 weeks of persistent low mood, tearfulness most days, sleep disruption beyond baby's feeds, feeling overwhelmed, and reduced enjoyment of her baby. She denies thoughts of harming the baby. There is no personal history of psychiatric illness. Her mother had postnatal depression.

She has no active suicidal plan or intent, no psychotic features, no acute safety concerns. Her partner is supportive and present. Social support is intact. Physical examination and thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), FBC and iron studies unremarkable
data_table.Assessment: EPDS 15, item 10 score 1 (occasional thoughts, no active plan), no psychosis, partner supportive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Advise her to stop breastfeeding immediately so that safe pharmacotherapy can be commenced without concern for infant exposure
options.rationale: Breastfeeding cessation is not required to treat PND; SSRIs including sertraline are safe with breastfeeding with minimal infant exposure. Discouraging breastfeeding worsens outcomes for both mother and baby. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal MH)

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg titrated to 50 mg daily monotherapy alone for depression without any psychological therapy referral in first-line management
options.rationale: SSRI monotherapy without psychological therapy is not first-line for moderate PND in a woman who has not previously tried psychological therapy; combined therapy is more effective than either alone if medication is used. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal MH)

options.text: Refer for structured psychological therapy (interpersonal therapy or CBT) with GP review in 2 weeks and safety plan for any escalation
options.rationale: Moderate postnatal depression (EPDS 15, no psychosis, no active suicidal intent) responds well to structured psychological therapy (interpersonal therapy or CBT) as first-line with GP follow-up. Medication is added if psychological therapy alone is insufficient or severity increases. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal MH)

options.text: Admit to a mother-baby unit involuntarily under the Mental Health Act for immediate psychiatric assessment and stabilisation
options.rationale: Involuntary admission for moderate PND without psychosis, active suicidal intent, or safety concern is disproportionate and not appropriate; her presentation is community-manageable with structured supports. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal MH)

options.text: Reassure her that this is baby blues and will resolve spontaneously in the next 2 weeks; follow up if not improving
options.rationale: Baby blues resolve within 10 to 14 days of delivery; symptoms lasting 4 weeks with EPDS 15 meet threshold for depression and require active management rather than reassurance. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal MH)

explanation.summary: The 6-week postnatal check is a national screening opportunity using EPDS. Score 13 or above suggests significant depressive symptoms warranting further assessment; item 10 (self-harm thoughts) requires safety assessment regardless of total score. Moderate PND is managed first-line with structured psychological therapy (interpersonal therapy or CBT); sertraline is the preferred SSRI if medication is added, being compatible with breastfeeding. Severe PND, psychotic features, or active suicidal or infanticidal thoughts warrant urgent perinatal psychiatry referral and consideration of mother-baby unit admission.
key_points: EPDS >=13 or item 10 positive: further assessment
First-line moderate PND: psychological therapy (IPT or CBT)
SSRI first choice if medication: sertraline (compatible with breastfeeding)
Escalate to perinatal psychiatry for severe, psychotic, or high-risk presentations
explanation.pearls: Sertraline lowest breastmilk transfer of SSRIs; paroxetine also low transfer. Fluoxetine has long half-life and higher infant plasma levels: avoid if starting anew in a lactating woman.
